name: Hassan Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics, and I share a cramped flat in Brindley with two flatmates, rent split three ways. Tuesday and Thursday I have lectures, and three nights a week I stock shelves at Lowmart from nine until two. Sleep is the first thing to go. The other days I'm in the library or on my phone doing the reading.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's it like so far, compared with what you pictured?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The maths is harder than school, and the lecturers assume you've already read everything. I use an AI tool now and then to explain a graph I didn't follow, but I check it against the textbook. The loan covers fees and my rent barely. Anything else comes from Lowmart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years there's a big claim that turns out to be half marketing. Economics students know about hype cycles, and I'd tell my flatmates the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays as tight as it is now. Rent goes up, wages don't, and I have under a month saved. The tech isn't the problem, the pricing of everything is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the night shifts and ask Lowmart for a fourth night if they offer. I'd also try tutoring maths to sixth-formers for fifteen pounds an hour, because that pays more per hour than stacking shelves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired but not afraid. Nothing is new here, so I'd just be carrying on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a bad month look like for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bad month is when the boiler breaks or my shift gets cut. Then I skip lectures to cover hours. I'd borrow from my flatmate Jonas, and I hate owing him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this picture change how you see your course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The course is fine in that world. I'd probably stay in economics and aim for a regular graduate job in a bank or the council.

say: I'd tell flatmates it's a **hype cycle** and every few years there's one.
I'd say rent and prices matter more than the tech.
think: My life stays **tight**: rent rises, wages don't, and savings sit under a month.
The tech isn't the problem, the **cost** of everything is.
do: Keep the **night shifts** and ask Lowmart for a fourth.
Tutor maths to sixth-formers for **fifteen pounds** an hour.
Aim for a regular graduate job after the degree.
feel: **Tired** but not afraid, because nothing new happens.
S0.quote: The tech isn't the problem, the pricing of everything is.
fieldNote: Reads the plateau as **continuity**, which suits his steady temperament.
Pressure comes from rent and a thin cushion, not AI.
Already sees tutoring as a better hourly rate than shelf stacking.

steps.text: Keep the three night shifts stocking shelves at Lowmart
Start tutoring maths to sixth-formers at fifteen pounds an hour
Cut takeaways and buy a cheaper weekly food shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and the question is who gets the gains. Without rules, a handful of firms collect the money and everyone else retrains on their own dime. I'd say that in seminars and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm more worried than I sound. Entry roles in banking and consultancy involve spreadsheets, research and reports. Those are the things the tools do now. The job I'm aiming at may shrink by the time I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI tools properly rather than now and then, and learn the ones firms actually use. I'd add a statistics course. I'd also keep the Lowmart shifts and join the shop workers' union, since checkout and stock jobs will change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's a bit like watching a queue get shorter and knowing I'm at the back of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of economics work would AI take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A graduate analyst spends the first year cleaning data and writing short briefs. Software can do a rough version now. By the time I graduate it will do a better one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should carry the cost if jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firms and the government together. If companies save money by cutting graduate hiring, they should pay in a training levy. I'd vote for whoever puts that in a manifesto.

say: I'd say the gains go to a **handful of firms** unless rules change.
I'd argue for a training **levy** on firms that cut graduate hiring.
think: Entry **analyst** roles are the ones the tools do best already.
The job I'm aiming at may be **smaller** by graduation.
do: Learn the AI tools firms really use, not just **dabble**.
Add a **statistics** module to my timetable.
Join the shop workers' **union** at Lowmart.
feel: **Anxious**, like watching a queue shrink while I'm at the back.
S1.quote: A graduate analyst spends the first year cleaning data and writing short briefs. Software can do a rough version now.
fieldNote: Gets **specific** about which entry tasks software will take.
Wants policy answers, a levy and training, not charity.
Moves from occasional AI use to deliberate learning.

steps.text: Learn the AI tools banks and consultancies use, starting this term
Add a statistics module to next year's timetable
Join the shop workers' union at Lowmart
Vote for a party promising a graduate training levy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs emergency policy. Taxes on AI profits, public ownership of the biggest systems, and income support. I'd post about it and go to a protest if there was one in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. I graduate in 2029, around when thinking jobs go. The wage I'm saving for would be worth nothing and I'd still owe the loan. I'd have maybe a year of study before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food. I'd keep stacking shelves because hands-on jobs last until about 2031. I'd also ask the careers office what jobs are still hiring, and maybe move into logistics or care if the degree looks pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the kind of fear where you re-do your plans at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you do about the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dropping economics is a loss, because I like it. But debt for a degree with no job at the end is a trap. I'd ask the money advice office whether I can pause the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Jonas, because we'd share the rent problem. Then my mum, who sends what she can, though I hate asking her.

say: I'd call for **taxes** on AI profits and income support.
I'd post about it and join a **protest** if one comes to town.
think: I graduate in **2029**, right when thinking jobs go, still owing the loan.
The wage I'm saving for could be worth **nothing**.
do: Spend only on rent and **food** from now on.
Keep the Lowmart **shifts** because hands-on jobs last longer.
Ask the careers office what is still **hiring**.
feel: **Alarmed**, re-doing my plans at three in the morning.
S2.quote: Dropping economics is a loss, because I like it. But debt for a degree with no job at the end is a trap.
fieldNote: Mixes **policy** thinking with real personal fear.
Sees hands-on work as the safer shelter, a smart reading of the timeline.
Loves the subject, so leaving would cost him emotionally.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and the bus pass
Keep the Lowmart night shifts through the next three years
Ask the money advice office if I can pause the loan
Go to a protest demanding taxes on AI profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get the rules right. Five years is just enough for governments to act if they start now. I'd keep saying so to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel I could manage it. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years before AGI. I could get a first job and some savings. The risk is that the first job doesn't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, use AI tools every week, and build a skill that is hands-on, like running a small project or sales. I'd also keep the tutoring side income. If the market looks dead near 2029, I'd think about a trade qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I have time to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is panic, and five is a plan. With five I can finish the degree, earn something, and see if the job market holds. Waiting costs nothing for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast on whatever the job market actually rewards. If analyst jobs have vanished, I'd go for operations roles. If they haven't, great, I'd keep going.

say: I'd say five years is **just enough** for governments to act if they start now.
I'd tell friends to plan, not panic.
think: I could **manage** this: a first job and some savings before it hits.
The risk is that my first job **doesn't last**.
do: Finish the degree and use AI tools **every week**.
Look at a **trade** qualification if the graduate market looks dead.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, because there is time to try things.
S3.quote: Two years is panic, and five is a plan. With five I can finish the degree, earn something, and see if the job market holds.
fieldNote: Willing to consider a trade, which he'd have rejected in the plateau case.
Keeps politics as a background habit.

steps.text: Use AI tools weekly on coursework to build real skill
Keep tutoring maths and save half of every payment
Research a trade qualification as a fallback by second year
Open a savings account and pay in monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is how long it took for the internet to change shops. We have time for rules and for schools to adapt. I'd be cautiously optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel pretty okay. By thirty I'd have a career, or at least a flexible skill set. The danger is that people ignore the date, then panic in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, add a data skill, maybe do a master's later if it pays. I'd use AI tools heavily, and I'd start saving properly once the loan situation settles. I'd also stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm fine in the long run, but the money stress now doesn't disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, economics is useful in any world because it teaches how to think about trade-offs. Even if jobs change, it helps me understand where the money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the degree still be the right choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time on useful side projects, like a small analytics business with a friend. Ten years lets you try and fail once or twice.

say: I'd say we have **time** for rules and for schools to adapt.
I'd tell flatmates the internet took years to change shops, and this will too.
think: I'd be fine by thirty with a **career** or a flexible skill set.
The danger is people **ignoring** the date, then panicking.
do: Finish the degree and add a **data skill**.
Use AI tools **heavily** from second year.
Start **saving** properly once the loan settles.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the money stress now doesn't go away.
S4.quote: Economics is useful in any world because it teaches how to think about trade-offs.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **optimistic** but the cushion keeps him uneasy.
Plans a side project with a friend, showing steady risk-taking.
Warns about people ignoring the deadline.

steps.text: Take a data analysis course next summer
Use AI tools on every assignment to build skill
Save fifty pounds a month once the loan stabilises
Start a small analytics project with a friend

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, the debt stays, and my graduation lands right on top of it. What would help is public rules, like a tax on AI profits and a basic income, and a way to pause student loans if the degree stops paying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that students on thin money think about this a lot. We're not naive about it. I'd like to see decision-makers spend a shift stacking shelves before they tell us to retrain.

headlineQuote: I'd like to see decision-makers spend a shift stacking shelves before they tell us to retrain.
portrait: Hassan is an eighteen-year-old **economics student** who shares a flat and stocks shelves three nights a week.
He's progressive and analytical, and he uses AI tools now and then to check graphs.
He blames big firms and weak rules rather than the technology itself.
He moves from sceptic to planner as the warning time grows, adding stats, tutoring and a union card.
His mood peaks at **alarmed** in the two-year case, with the loan still to pay.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, with debt still owed and graduation landing on top of it.
whatWouldHelp: A tax on **AI profits**, basic income and a way to pause student loans.
Decision-makers who understand **shift work** before they advise retraining.
